title: Pharmacology Core
summary: How drugs get in, act, and leave the body, how to read an order and do the math, and the drug classes you will hand to a nurse or watch go in during an emergency department shift.

lessons.title: Getting in: absorption, routes, and where the drug goes
lessons.body:
## Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug

Four things happen to every drug: it gets in (absorption), it travels (distribution), it gets chemically changed (metabolism), and it leaves (elimination). Memorize them as ADME. Together they predict how fast a drug works, how long it lasts, and who it will hurt.

## Absorption and bioavailability

Absorption is the drug crossing from where you put it into the bloodstream. Bioavailability is the fraction that actually arrives intact and able to work. An IV drug skips absorption entirely, so IV bioavailability is `100%` by definition. A swallowed pill may deliver anywhere from `5%` to `90%`.

Morphine is the clean example. Only about `25%` to `30%` of a swallowed dose survives the trip, which is why `10 mg` IV morphine and `30 mg` oral morphine relieve roughly the same amount of pain.

## Routes ranked by how fast they work

| Route | Typical onset | Why |
|---|---|---|
| IV | seconds to 1 min | straight into the circulation |
| IO (intraosseous) | seconds to 1 min | marrow is a vein that cannot collapse |
| Inhaled or nebulized | 1-5 min | enormous alveolar surface area |
| Sublingual (SL) | 1-3 min | rich mucosal veins, skips the liver |
| Intranasal (IN) | 3-5 min | mucosa drains straight to blood |
| IM | 5-20 min | muscle is well perfused |
| SubQ | 15-30 min | fat is poorly perfused |
| Rectal (PR) | 5-30 min | partial liver bypass |
| Oral (PO) | 30-90 min | must dissolve, absorb, survive the liver |
| Transdermal | hours | designed to be slow and steady |

> **Key:** In shock the body shuts down perfusion to skin, fat, and muscle, so IM and SubQ drugs sit in the tissue unabsorbed. That is why anaphylaxis gets `0.3 mg` of `1 mg/mL` epinephrine IM into the outer thigh rather than SubQ, and why SubQ insulin is unreliable in diabetic ketoacidosis.

## The first-pass effect

Blood leaving the stomach and intestine does not go to the body first. It goes to the liver through the portal vein. The liver can destroy a large share of the dose on that single trip before the drug ever reaches the heart. That is the first-pass effect.

Sublingual nitroglycerin exists because of it. Swallowed nitroglycerin is almost completely destroyed on the first pass and does nothing. Placed under the tongue, it absorbs into mucosal veins that drain to the superior vena cava, bypasses the liver, and relieves chest pain in `1` to `3` minutes. Rectal and transdermal routes bypass the portal system partially for the same reason.

## Distribution

Once in the blood, a drug spreads. Well-perfused organs (brain, heart, kidneys, liver) see it within a minute; fat, skin, and bone see it last. Volume of distribution is the shorthand for how widely it spreads. A drug that stays in the bloodstream has a small volume of distribution. Digoxin buries itself in muscle and tissue, so its volume of distribution is huge, which is exactly why it needs a loading dose.

## Protein binding

Many drugs ride through the blood stuck to albumin. Only the free, unbound portion can reach a receptor and act. Warfarin is about `99%` bound, so only `1%` is working. If albumin falls (cirrhosis, malnutrition, critical illness) or another drug competes for the same binding sites, the free fraction can double with no change in the dose, and the patient bleeds.

## The blood-brain barrier

Brain capillaries are sealed with tight junctions, so only small, fat-loving (lipophilic) molecules cross easily. Fentanyl is extremely lipophilic and reaches the brain in under a minute. Diphenhydramine crosses and sedates; loratadine barely crosses and does not. Glycopyrrolate does not cross, while atropine does, which is why atropine can leave an older patient confused and agitated.
keyPoints: ADME: absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination — the four questions every drug faces.
IV bioavailability is 100%; oral morphine is only about 25-30%, so 10 mg IV equals roughly 30 mg PO.
First-pass metabolism destroys swallowed nitroglycerin, so it is given sublingually and works in 1-3 minutes.
In shock, IM and SubQ absorption fails because perfusion to muscle and fat collapses.
Only unbound drug works: warfarin is 99% albumin-bound, so small binding shifts cause big effects.

checks.q: A patient in anaphylaxis gets epinephrine IM in the lateral thigh rather than SubQ. The main reason is:
choices: Muscle is far better perfused than fat, so absorption is faster and more reliable
The IM dose is smaller and therefore safer
Subcutaneous fat chemically destroys epinephrine
IM injections hurt less than SubQ injections
checks.why: Absorption depends on blood flow. Muscle has much richer perfusion than subcutaneous fat, and in shock the fat is shut down first. The IM dose (0.3 mg of 1 mg/mL) is not smaller, epinephrine is not destroyed in fat, and comfort is irrelevant.

checks.q: Nitroglycerin for chest pain is placed under the tongue instead of swallowed because sublingual delivery:
choices: Increases the total dose absorbed over 24 hours
Bypasses the liver, avoiding near-total destruction on the first pass
Avoids stomach acid, which is what destroys nitroglycerin
Allows a slower, steadier release
checks.why: Swallowed nitroglycerin drains to the liver through the portal vein and is almost entirely metabolized before reaching the circulation. Sublingual veins drain to the superior vena cava instead. The problem is hepatic first-pass metabolism, not acid, and the point is speed (1-3 minutes), not slow release.

checks.q: A cirrhotic patient on a stable warfarin dose develops a very low albumin. What happens to the drug effect?
choices: Nothing, because the prescribed dose has not changed
Effect falls, because less drug is carried to the tissues
Effect rises, because a larger fraction of the drug is free and active
Effect rises, because albumin is the receptor for warfarin
checks.why: Only unbound drug is active. Warfarin is roughly 99% albumin-bound, so less albumin means more free warfarin and more anticoagulation at the same dose. Albumin is a carrier, not a receptor, and low albumin does not reduce delivery of a highly bound drug.

lessons.title: Getting out: the liver, the kidneys, and half-life
lessons.body:
## Metabolism: the liver makes drugs excretable

Most drugs are fat-soluble, and the kidney can only flush out water-soluble things. The liver's job is to convert one into the other. Phase I reactions (mostly oxidation by the cytochrome P450 enzyme family, written CYP) add or uncover a chemical handle. Phase II reactions (conjugation) bolt a water-loving group onto that handle, and the kidney dumps it.

Some drugs arrive inactive and the liver switches them on. These are prodrugs. Codeine does nothing until CYP2D6 converts about `10%` of it into morphine, so people missing the enzyme get no relief and ultra-fast metabolizers can get a dangerous amount. Clopidogrel is also a prodrug, activated by CYP2C19.

## Inhibitors and inducers, the whole idea in two lines

Picture the CYP enzymes as a workforce clearing drugs off a loading dock.

- An **inhibitor** fires the workers. The other drug piles up. Levels rise, often within a day. Risk: toxicity.
- An **inducer** hires more workers. Over days to weeks the other drug is cleared faster. Levels fall. Risk: treatment failure.

Common inhibitors: amiodarone, azole antifungals (fluconazole, ketoconazole), clarithromycin and erythromycin (azithromycin is the safe one), ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, cimetidine, ritonavir, and grapefruit juice.

Common inducers: rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St. John's wort, and chronic alcohol use.

> **Key:** Inhibitors push the other drug up toward toxicity. Inducers push it down toward failure — including failure of oral contraceptives in a patient started on rifampin.

Grapefruit juice blocks CYP3A4 in the intestinal wall, so less of the dose is destroyed during absorption and more reaches the blood. With simvastatin that can multiply exposure several-fold and trigger muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis).

Warfarin is the classic victim because it is cleared by CYP2C9 and has almost no margin for error. Add fluconazole, metronidazole, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or amiodarone and the INR climbs toward bleeding. Add rifampin and the INR falls toward clotting.

## Elimination and half-life

Half-life is the time it takes for the blood concentration to fall by half. Two rules do almost all the work:

1. After the last dose, a drug is essentially gone in `4` to `5` half-lives (about `94%` to `97%` cleared).
2. On a fixed repeating dose, the level plateaus (steady state) after `4` to `5` half-lives.

So a drug with a `12`-hour half-life needs `2` to `2.5` days to reach a stable level, and the same `2` to `2.5` days before a dose change shows its full effect. Drawing a level sooner tells you very little.

## Loading dose versus maintenance dose

When you cannot wait four half-lives, give a **loading dose**: one large dose that fills the volume of distribution right away. After that a **maintenance dose** simply replaces what is eliminated.

- Loading dose is set by volume of distribution.
- Maintenance dose is set by clearance, meaning kidney and liver function.

Real examples: fosphenytoin `15-20 mg/kg` load then maintenance, vancomycin `25-30 mg/kg` load in severe sepsis, heparin `80 units/kg` bolus then `18 units/kg/h`, amiodarone `150 mg` over 10 minutes then a drip.

## Who needs a different dose

Failing kidneys let renally cleared drugs stack up: vancomycin, gentamicin, enoxaparin, metformin, digoxin, gabapentin, and most beta-lactams. The dose is cut or the interval stretched based on creatinine clearance.

Failing liver does the same for hepatically cleared drugs. The acetaminophen ceiling drops from `4 g` to `2-3 g` per day, and benzodiazepines and opioids last far longer than expected.

Older adults have lower glomerular filtration, less albumin, and more body fat, so the rule is start low and go slow; the Beers criteria list drugs to avoid after `65` (diphenhydramine, benzodiazepines, chronic NSAIDs). Children dose by weight in kilograms, and newborns have immature enzymes. In pregnancy the absolute avoid list is ACE inhibitors and ARBs, warfarin, isotretinoin, tetracyclines, and fluoroquinolones.
keyPoints: Phase I (CYP450 oxidation) then Phase II (conjugation) turn fat-soluble drugs into water-soluble waste.
CYP inhibitors raise the other drug's level toward toxicity; inducers lower it toward treatment failure.
Grapefruit blocks intestinal CYP3A4 and raises bioavailability — the statin and rhabdomyolysis problem.
4 to 5 half-lives to be gone, and 4 to 5 half-lives to reach steady state on a fixed dose.
Loading dose fills the volume of distribution; maintenance dose matches clearance (kidney and liver).

checks.q: A patient stable on warfarin with an INR of 2.4 is started on fluconazole for a yeast infection. What should you expect?
choices: INR falls, because fluconazole induces CYP2C9
INR rises, because fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9 and warfarin accumulates
No change, because fluconazole is not metabolized by the liver
INR rises, because fluconazole itself thins the blood
checks.why: Fluconazole is a CYP inhibitor, so warfarin clearance falls and the free drug accumulates, pushing the INR up and the patient toward bleeding. Rifampin is the inducer that does the opposite. Fluconazole has no direct anticoagulant activity of its own.

checks.q: A drug has a half-life of 8 hours and is dosed every 8 hours. About how long until the blood level reaches steady state?
choices: 8 hours
16 hours
32 to 40 hours
8 days
checks.why: Steady state arrives after 4 to 5 half-lives regardless of dosing interval, so 4 to 5 times 8 hours is 32 to 40 hours. One or two half-lives is only 50% to 75% of the way there, and 8 days would be 24 half-lives.

checks.q: Why does a patient in severe sepsis get vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg as a first dose and a smaller dose after?
choices: The loading dose fills the volume of distribution immediately instead of waiting 4-5 half-lives
The first dose is larger because bacteria are most resistant early
Larger first doses reduce kidney injury
The loading dose is calculated from creatinine clearance and the maintenance dose is not
checks.why: A loading dose is sized to the volume of distribution so therapeutic levels arrive now rather than after four half-lives. Maintenance dosing is the part adjusted for clearance and kidney function, and larger vancomycin exposure increases, not decreases, nephrotoxicity risk.

lessons.title: Receptors: how a drug actually does something
lessons.body:
## Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body

Almost every drug works by grabbing a protein called a receptor, the way a key fits a lock. What happens next divides drugs into a few types you will use every day.

- **Agonist**: binds and turns the receptor on. Albuterol on beta-2, morphine on mu.
- **Antagonist**: binds and blocks, producing no effect itself. Naloxone on mu, metoprolol on beta-1.
- **Partial agonist**: binds and turns the receptor partly on, with a ceiling it cannot exceed. Buprenorphine on mu.

Naloxone is a pure competitive antagonist with a high affinity for the mu receptor, so it shoves opioids off. Dose `0.4 mg` to `2 mg` IV, onset `1` to `2` minutes, but its duration is only `30` to `90` minutes, shorter than most opioids. That mismatch is why a patient can wake up, then go back to sleep and stop breathing an hour later.

Buprenorphine shows the partial agonist idea. Its ceiling on respiratory depression makes it comparatively safe, but its receptor grip is so strong that giving it to someone with a full agonist on board can rip that opioid off and precipitate withdrawal.

## Potency is not efficacy

**Potency** is how much drug you need. **Efficacy** is the biggest effect the drug can produce no matter how much you give.

Fentanyl `100 mcg` gives about the same analgesia as morphine `10 mg`, so fentanyl is roughly `100` times more potent. It is not more effective; both are full mu agonists that can relieve severe pain. Ketorolac is quite potent for an anti-inflammatory but its ceiling is genuinely lower, so no amount of it equals morphine in a femur fracture.

> **Trap:** Exam questions love to call the more potent drug the stronger drug. Potency only sets the number on the syringe. Efficacy sets how much pain can actually be taken away.

## Dose-response and therapeutic index

Plot effect against dose and you get an S-shaped curve. ED50 is the dose that produces the desired effect in half of patients; TD50 is the dose that produces toxicity in half. Therapeutic index is TD50 divided by ED50 — the size of the safety gap.

A wide index means a sloppy dose is still safe. A narrow index means small changes in level cause toxicity, so these drugs get blood levels drawn:

| Drug | Therapeutic range |
|---|---|
| Digoxin | `0.5-2.0 ng/mL` |
| Lithium | `0.6-1.2 mEq/L` |
| Phenytoin | `10-20 mcg/mL` total |
| Warfarin | INR `2-3` for most indications |
| Theophylline | `5-15 mcg/mL` |
| Vancomycin | trough `15-20 mcg/mL` for serious infection |

## Tolerance and dependence

**Tolerance** is needing more drug for the same effect, usually because receptors downregulate. **Tachyphylaxis** is tolerance that develops in hours, which is why a nitroglycerin drip loses effect and needs a nitrate-free interval. **Physical dependence** means withdrawal symptoms on stopping, which is a predictable body response and not the same thing as addiction, a behavioral disease of compulsive use despite harm.

## The receptor families that organize everything

| Receptor | Turning it on does | Drugs |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha-1 | vasoconstriction, raises blood pressure | phenylephrine, norepinephrine |
| Alpha-2 | dampens sympathetic outflow, sedation | clonidine, dexmedetomidine |
| Beta-1 | faster, harder heartbeat | dobutamine; blocked by metoprolol |
| Beta-2 | bronchodilation, vessel dilation | albuterol, terbutaline |
| Muscarinic | rest and digest: slow heart, secretions | blocked by atropine, glycopyrrolate |
| Nicotinic | skeletal muscle contraction | blocked by rocuronium |
| Opioid mu | analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression | morphine, fentanyl; blocked by naloxone |
| Opioid kappa | analgesia with dysphoria | butorphanol |
| GABA-A | chloride in, neuron quiet, sedation | benzodiazepines, propofol, alcohol |
| Histamine H1 | itch, hives, wheeze, wakefulness | blocked by diphenhydramine, cetirizine |
| Histamine H2 | stomach acid secretion | blocked by famotidine |
| Dopamine D2 | movement, reward, vomiting trigger | blocked by haloperidol, metoclopramide |
| Serotonin 5-HT3 | vomiting reflex | blocked by ondansetron |
| NMDA (glutamate) | excitation, pain wind-up | blocked by ketamine |
keyPoints: Agonist turns a receptor on, antagonist blocks it, partial agonist turns it partly on with a ceiling.
Naloxone lasts 30-90 minutes, shorter than most opioids, so re-sedation is the danger.
Potency is the dose needed; efficacy is the maximum achievable effect — fentanyl is 100x more potent than morphine, not stronger.
Narrow therapeutic index drugs get levels drawn: digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, warfarin, theophylline, vancomycin.
Alpha-1 constricts, beta-1 drives the heart, beta-2 opens airways, mu gives analgesia and apnea, GABA-A sedates.

checks.q: An opioid overdose patient wakes after naloxone 0.4 mg IV. Forty minutes later he is unresponsive and breathing 6 times a minute again. The best explanation is:
choices: Naloxone caused rebound respiratory depression
He developed sudden tolerance to naloxone
Naloxone's duration of 30-90 minutes is shorter than the opioid's, so the opioid re-occupied the receptors
The original dose of naloxone was too high and saturated the receptors
checks.why: Naloxone is a short-acting competitive antagonist. When it washes out, the longer-acting opioid still circulating re-binds mu receptors and apnea returns, which is why these patients need observation or a drip. Naloxone itself causes no respiratory depression and tolerance does not develop in minutes.

checks.q: Which pairing correctly matches a receptor to its effect?
choices: Beta-2 stimulation constricts the bronchi
Alpha-1 stimulation constricts blood vessels and raises blood pressure
Muscarinic blockade slows the heart rate
Mu agonism increases respiratory drive
checks.why: Alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle constrict vessels, which is how phenylephrine and norepinephrine raise pressure. Beta-2 dilates bronchi, muscarinic blockade with atropine speeds the heart, and mu agonists depress respiratory drive.

checks.q: A nitroglycerin drip that controlled a patient's chest pain at 20 mcg/min stops working after 18 hours at the same rate. This is:
choices: Tachyphylaxis, rapid tolerance that requires a nitrate-free interval
A narrow therapeutic index effect
Physical dependence
Loss of potency with no loss of efficacy
checks.why: Nitrate tolerance develops within hours of continuous infusion, the textbook example of tachyphylaxis, and is managed with a nitrate-free interval. Dependence refers to withdrawal on stopping, and therapeutic index describes the gap between effective and toxic doses, not fading response.

lessons.title: Reading the order and doing the math
lessons.body:
## An order has five parts

Every complete medication order names the **drug**, the **dose**, the **route**, the **frequency**, and the **indication**. If one is missing, the order is not safe to carry out.

| Abbreviation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| PO | by mouth |
| IV / IM / SubQ / IO | into vein / muscle / fat / bone |
| SL / PR / IN | under tongue / rectal / intranasal |
| PRN | as needed |
| STAT | immediately |
| q6h | every 6 hours |
| BID / TID / QID | 2, 3, 4 times a day |
| gtt | drop (gtt/min is drops per minute) |
| mcg | microgram, one thousandth of a milligram |
| mEq | milliequivalent (electrolytes) |

Dangerous abbreviations are banned in most hospitals: U for units (looks like a zero), QD for daily (looks like QID), and a trailing zero such as `1.0 mg` (reads as `10 mg`). Always write `0.5 mg`, never `.5 mg`.

## The four pieces of math

**1. Weight-based dosing.** Doses are per kilogram, never pounds. Pounds divided by `2.2` gives kilograms. A `176 lb` patient is `80 kg`.

**2. Milligrams to milliliters.** Volume equals dose divided by concentration.

**3. Percent solutions and ratios.** A `1%` solution is `1 g` per `100 mL`, which is `10 mg/mL`. So lidocaine `2%` is `20 mg/mL` and D50 is `50 g/100 mL`, meaning `25 g` of dextrose in the `50 mL` syringe. Epinephrine `1 mg/mL` is the old `1:1,000` (anaphylaxis, IM); epinephrine `0.1 mg/mL` is the old `1:10,000` (cardiac arrest, IV).

**4. Infusion rates.** Rate in `mL/h` equals the ordered amount per hour divided by the bag concentration. With a gravity set, drops per minute equals `mL/h` times the set's drip factor divided by `60`.

## Three worked examples

**Example 1 — weight-based push.** Order: fentanyl `1 mcg/kg` IV once for a `176 lb` patient. Vial is `100 mcg/2 mL`.

1. Weight: `176 / 2.2 = 80 kg`.
2. Dose: `80 kg x 1 mcg/kg = 80 mcg`.
3. Concentration: `100 mcg / 2 mL = 50 mcg/mL`.
4. Volume: `80 / 50 = 1.6 mL`.

**Example 2 — infusion rate.** Order: heparin `18 units/kg/h` for the same `80 kg` patient. Bag is `25,000 units in 250 mL`.

1. Dose per hour: `80 x 18 = 1,440 units/h`.
2. Concentration: `25,000 / 250 = 100 units/mL`.
3. Rate: `1,440 / 100 = 14.4 mL/h`.

**Example 3 — pediatric fluids and drip factor.** A `30 kg` child needs maintenance fluid on a `15 gtt/mL` set. Use the 4-2-1 rule: `4 mL/kg/h` for the first `10 kg`, `2 mL/kg/h` for the next `10 kg`, `1 mL/kg/h` for every kilogram after that.

1. `(10 x 4) + (10 x 2) + (10 x 1) = 40 + 20 + 10 = 70 mL/h`.
2. Drops: `70 x 15 / 60 = 17.5`, so `18 gtt/min`.
3. If that child were in shock instead, the bolus is `20 mL/kg = 600 mL` of isotonic crystalloid, rapidly. Adults get `20-30 mL/kg`.

## High-alert medications

A short list of drugs causes most of the deaths from medication error, so they get an independent double check by a second licensed person before they go in: insulin, IV heparin and other anticoagulants, opioids, concentrated electrolytes, chemotherapy, and neuromuscular blockers.

> **Key:** Concentrated potassium chloride is never given IV push. Ever. It stops the heart. It goes in a bag, diluted, at no more than `10 mEq/h` peripherally or `20 mEq/h` through a central line with cardiac monitoring.

> **On shift:** A paralytic drawn up and left unlabeled next to a sedative has killed patients. Label every syringe, and never hand off an unlabeled one.
keyPoints: A complete order has drug, dose, route, frequency, and indication — five parts, no exceptions.
1% solution is 10 mg/mL; lidocaine 2% is 20 mg/mL; epinephrine 1 mg/mL is IM, 0.1 mg/mL is IV.
Volume equals dose divided by concentration; mL/h equals hourly dose divided by bag concentration.
4-2-1 rule for maintenance fluid: 4 mL/kg/h first 10 kg, 2 for the next 10, 1 for each kg beyond.
Concentrated potassium chloride is never IV push; high-alert drugs get an independent double check.

checks.q: Order: morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV for a 110 lb patient. The vial reads 10 mg/mL. What volume do you draw?
choices: 0.5 mL
1.1 mL
5 mL
checks.why: 110 lb divided by 2.2 is 50 kg, times 0.1 mg/kg is 5 mg. At 10 mg/mL, 5 mg is 0.5 mL. Answer 1.1 mL comes from using pounds, and 5 mL comes from confusing the dose in mg with a volume in mL.

checks.q: A 20 kg child in septic shock needs a fluid bolus. The correct volume is:
choices: 60 mL, which is the 4-2-1 maintenance rate
400 to 600 mL, which is 20 to 30 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid
1,000 mL, the standard adult bolus
200 mL, which is 10 mL/kg
checks.why: Pediatric shock boluses are weight-based at 20 mL/kg, so 20 kg gets 400 mL, repeated as needed. The 4-2-1 rule gives an hourly maintenance rate of 60 mL/h, not a bolus, and a fixed adult liter would be a large overdose in a 20 kg child.

checks.q: Which statement about concentrated potassium chloride is correct?
choices: It may be pushed IV slowly over 2 minutes if the patient is on a monitor
It is never given IV push; it must be diluted and infused, no faster than about 10 mEq/h peripherally
It is safe to push if the potassium is below 2.5 mEq/L
It is a high-alert drug only in pediatric patients
checks.why: Undiluted potassium chloride given by push causes immediate cardiac arrest, so the rule is absolute regardless of monitoring, the potassium level, or patient age. It is infused diluted, roughly 10 mEq/h peripherally and up to 20 mEq/h centrally with monitoring.

lessons.title: Pain drugs: acetaminophen, NSAIDs, opioids, and locals
lessons.body:
## Acetaminophen

Acetaminophen blocks prostaglandin production mostly inside the central nervous system, so it treats pain and fever but not inflammation. Adult dose is `650-1000 mg` every `6` hours, ceiling `4 g` in 24 hours and `2-3 g` if there is liver disease, heavy alcohol use, or malnutrition. Children get `15 mg/kg` per dose.

Overdose is the danger. Normally a small fraction becomes a toxic metabolite called NAPQI, which glutathione neutralizes. In overdose glutathione runs out, NAPQI attacks liver cells, and the patient looks well for `24` hours before liver failure appears on day `3` or `4`. The antidote, N-acetylcysteine, restores glutathione and is near-perfect if started within `8` hours. A `4`-hour level plotted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram decides treatment.

> **Trap:** Hundreds of combination products hide acetaminophen (oxycodone-acetaminophen, cold remedies). Accidental overdose usually comes from stacking products, not from one big swallow.

## NSAIDs

NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase, so less prostaglandin means less inflammation, pain, and fever. The same blockade removes the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining and keep the kidney's afferent arteriole open. That gives the three classic harms: GI ulcer and bleeding, acute kidney injury, and bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma.

Ibuprofen `400-600 mg` PO. Ketorolac `15-30 mg` IV, using `15 mg` if the patient is over `65`, under `50 kg`, or has any kidney impairment, and never longer than `5` days. Kidney risk multiplies when an NSAID meets a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor in a dehydrated patient. Avoid in the third trimester of pregnancy and after coronary bypass surgery.

## Opioids

Opioids are mu receptor agonists. They dull pain perception, produce euphoria, and — the part that kills — reduce the brainstem's drive to breathe. Constipation, itching, nausea, and miosis (pinpoint pupils) round out the picture, and tolerance develops to everything except constipation.

| Drug | Typical adult IV dose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Morphine | `0.1 mg/kg` or `2-4 mg` | histamine release causes itch and hypotension; metabolites build up in kidney failure |
| Hydromorphone | `0.5-1 mg` | roughly `5-7` times morphine's potency, a common error source |
| Fentanyl | `50-100 mcg` | onset `1-2` min, lasts `30-60` min, no histamine, safest in hypotension and kidney failure |
| Oxycodone | `5-10 mg` PO | oral only |

Rough equivalence: morphine `10 mg` IV equals hydromorphone `1.5 mg` IV equals fentanyl `100 mcg` IV equals morphine `30 mg` PO. Fentanyl is about `100` times as potent as morphine by weight, which is why illicit fentanyl kills at doses invisible to the eye.

Naloxone `0.4-2 mg` IV, IM, or IN reverses it. Start low in a chronic opioid user to avoid dumping them into withdrawal, and watch for re-sedation once naloxone wears off in `30-90` minutes.

## Ketamine for pain

At low analgesic doses, `0.1-0.3 mg/kg` IV given over `10-15` minutes, ketamine blocks NMDA receptors and relieves severe pain without dropping blood pressure or respiratory drive. Pushed fast it causes an unpleasant dissociative feeling, so it is infused, not slammed.

## Local anesthetics

Lidocaine blocks sodium channels in nerves so the signal never leaves the wound. `1%` is `10 mg/mL`; maximum is `4.5 mg/kg` plain or `7 mg/kg` with epinephrine, because the epinephrine constricts vessels and slows absorption while extending the block. Bupivacaine lasts `4-8` hours but is the most cardiotoxic. Systemic toxicity starts with tingling lips, metallic taste, and ringing ears, then seizures and arrhythmia; the rescue is IV lipid emulsion.

> **On shift:** Buffering lidocaine with sodium bicarbonate and injecting slowly with a small needle hurts far less, and that is usually the tech's job to set up.
keyPoints: Acetaminophen ceiling is 4 g/day, 2-3 g with liver disease; overdose is treated with N-acetylcysteine, best within 8 hours.
NSAIDs cause GI bleeding, acute kidney injury, and bronchospasm; ketorolac is 15 mg IV if over 65, under 50 kg, or renally impaired.
Hydromorphone is 5-7 times as potent as morphine and fentanyl about 100 times — the classic dosing error.
Fentanyl is the opioid of choice in hypotension and kidney failure; morphine releases histamine and accumulates.
Lidocaine max is 4.5 mg/kg plain, 7 mg/kg with epinephrine; local anesthetic toxicity is rescued with lipid emulsion.

checks.q: A patient took 25 acetaminophen tablets 3 hours ago and feels completely fine. The correct interpretation is:
choices: He is fine because he is asymptomatic and had a small ingestion
Feeling well early is expected; liver failure appears on day 3-4, so he needs a 4-hour level and likely N-acetylcysteine
He needs naloxone
Symptoms would already be obvious if this were a toxic dose
checks.why: The acetaminophen-poisoned patient looks well for about 24 hours while NAPQI destroys hepatocytes silently. A 4-hour level on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram guides N-acetylcysteine, which is nearly fully protective within 8 hours. Naloxone treats opioids, not acetaminophen.

checks.q: A 70-year-old on lisinopril and furosemide with mild chronic kidney disease has renal colic. Which analgesic choice is the most dangerous?
choices: Fentanyl 50 mcg IV
Acetaminophen 1000 mg PO
Ketorolac 30 mg IV
Lidocaine infiltration
checks.why: An NSAID plus an ACE inhibitor plus a diuretic in a dehydrated older patient with existing kidney disease is the classic combination for acute kidney injury, and 30 mg is twice the appropriate dose for someone over 65. Fentanyl and acetaminophen are far safer here.

checks.q: Which opioid is generally preferred for a hypotensive patient in kidney failure?
choices: Fentanyl, because it causes no histamine release and has no active renal metabolites
Morphine, because it is the standard reference opioid
Hydromorphone, because it is more potent
Oxycodone, because the oral route avoids the kidney
checks.why: Morphine releases histamine, which drops blood pressure further, and its active metabolites accumulate when the kidneys fail, causing prolonged sedation. Fentanyl avoids both problems. Potency and route do not address the underlying issue.

lessons.title: Sedatives, paralytics, and the brain drugs
lessons.body:
## Benzodiazepines

Benzodiazepines make the GABA-A receptor open more often, letting chloride into the neuron and quieting it. That single mechanism explains every use: stopping seizures, calming agitation, treating alcohol withdrawal, and sedating for procedures.

Lorazepam `2-4 mg` IV is the standard seizure dose (`0.1 mg/kg`, up to `4 mg` per dose). Midazolam `10 mg` IM is the choice when there is no IV, because it absorbs well from muscle. Diazepam works fast but redistributes into fat and has a very long tail.

> **Key:** Benzodiazepines and opioids together depress breathing far more than either alone. Most fatal overdoses involve both. Flumazenil, the reversal agent, is rarely used because it can strip GABA inhibition from a chronic user or a tricyclic co-ingestion and cause seizures nobody can stop.

## Drugs that stop seizures for longer

After benzodiazepines, a longer-acting antiepileptic is loaded: levetiracetam `60 mg/kg` up to `4,500 mg`, fosphenytoin `20 mg PE/kg`, or valproate `40 mg/kg`. Levetiracetam is favored because it has few interactions and does not drop blood pressure. Phenytoin must run slowly, no faster than `50 mg/min`, or it causes hypotension and arrhythmia, and it injures tissue if it leaks out of the vein.

## Antipsychotics and the agitated patient

Haloperidol and droperidol block dopamine D2 receptors; olanzapine blocks several receptors at once. Haloperidol `5 mg` IM or olanzapine `10 mg` IM calms severe agitation in `15-30` minutes.

The side effects come from the same D2 blockade. Dystonia is a sudden muscle spasm of the neck, jaw, or eyes, treated with diphenhydramine `25-50 mg` IV or benztropine `1-2 mg`. Akathisia is an unbearable inner restlessness. All of these drugs prolong the QT interval, and droperidol carries a boxed warning for it. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is the rare, deadly version: rigidity, fever, and confusion over days.

The old combination nicknamed the B52 is haloperidol `5 mg`, lorazepam `2 mg`, and diphenhydramine `50 mg` IM. Do not stack IM olanzapine with an IM benzodiazepine; the pair causes dangerous respiratory depression.

Ketamine `4-5 mg/kg` IM or `1-2 mg/kg` IV is the fastest option for extreme agitation, dissociating the patient in `2-5` minutes. Watch for laryngospasm and vomiting, and expect emergence reactions on the way out.

## Psychiatric drugs you must recognize

SSRIs (sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram) are safe alone but combine badly. Adding tramadol, linezolid, triptans, or an MAO inhibitor can cause serotonin syndrome: agitation, hyperreflexia, clonus that is worst in the legs, sweating, and fever, coming on within hours. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome looks similar but develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity and no clonus.

Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline) block sodium channels in overdose. The QRS widens past `100 ms`, seizures and hypotension follow, and the antidote is sodium bicarbonate `1-2 mEq/kg` IV push. Lithium has a narrow range of `0.6-1.2 mEq/L`, and NSAIDs, thiazides, and ACE inhibitors all push the level up toward tremor, confusion, and dialysis.

Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist that sedates without depressing respiration, which makes it useful in an intubated or withdrawing patient, at the cost of bradycardia and hypotension.

## Rapid sequence intubation

RSI is a sedative and a paralytic given back to back so the tube goes in on the first attempt.

| Drug | Dose | The one thing |
|---|---|---|
| Etomidate | `0.3 mg/kg` | barely touches blood pressure; brief adrenal suppression |
| Ketamine | `1-2 mg/kg` | supports blood pressure; good in shock and asthma |
| Propofol | `1.5-2.5 mg/kg` | drops blood pressure hard |
| Succinylcholine | `1.5 mg/kg` | works in `45-60` s, wears off in `6-10` min; forbidden in hyperkalemia, burns or crush over `48` hours old, spinal cord injury, or malignant hyperthermia history |
| Rocuronium | `1.2 mg/kg` | works in `60` s, lasts `45-60` min; reversed by sugammadex `16 mg/kg` |

> **On shift:** Before the drugs are pushed, the tech has suction on and tested, a bag-valve-mask ready, the monitor and waveform capnography on, two working IVs, the tube and a backup size open, and a push-dose pressor drawn.
keyPoints: Benzodiazepines open GABA-A chloride channels; lorazepam 2-4 mg IV or midazolam 10 mg IM stops seizures.
Benzodiazepine plus opioid is the lethal combination; flumazenil can cause unstoppable seizures and is rarely used.
D2 blockade calms agitation but causes dystonia, akathisia, and QT prolongation; dystonia is treated with diphenhydramine.
Serotonin syndrome comes on in hours with clonus; tricyclic overdose widens the QRS and needs sodium bicarbonate.
Succinylcholine is banned in hyperkalemia, burns or crush injury over 48 hours old, and malignant hyperthermia history.

checks.q: A patient on sertraline is given tramadol and hours later has agitation, sweating, hyperreflexia, ankle clonus, and a temperature of 39.4 C. The most likely diagnosis is:
choices: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Anticholinergic toxicity
Alcohol withdrawal
checks.why: Serotonin syndrome develops within hours of adding a serotonergic drug such as tramadol and is defined by neuromuscular excitation: clonus and hyperreflexia, worst in the legs. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity and no clonus, and anticholinergic toxicity gives dry skin with normal reflexes.

checks.q: A patient with a crush injury from three days ago needs intubation. Which paralytic is contraindicated and why?
choices: Rocuronium, because it lasts too long
Succinylcholine, because it can trigger a lethal potassium rise in crush injury older than about 48 hours
Succinylcholine, because it causes prolonged paralysis in muscle injury
Rocuronium, because there is no reversal agent
checks.why: Succinylcholine depolarizes muscle and releases potassium, and upregulated receptors after burns, crush injury, or denervation beyond roughly 48 hours can produce hyperkalemic arrest. Rocuronium is the safe alternative here and is reversible with sugammadex.

checks.q: An overdose patient has a QRS of 140 ms, hypotension, and a bottle of amitriptyline in the bag. The key treatment is:
choices: Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV
Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV
Naloxone 2 mg IV
Calcium gluconate 1 g IV
checks.why: Tricyclics block cardiac sodium channels, widening the QRS; sodium bicarbonate provides a sodium load and alkalinizes, which reverses the blockade. Flumazenil is specifically dangerous with tricyclics because it can provoke seizures, and naloxone and calcium do not address sodium channel blockade.

lessons.title: Antibiotics: what each class covers and what it costs
lessons.body:
## Two questions for every antibiotic

What does it cover, and what is its signature harm? Bacteria sort roughly into gram-positive (staph, strep, enterococcus), gram-negative (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas), atypical (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia), and anaerobes (the gut and mouth organisms that live without oxygen). Antibiotics either kill the cell wall, jam the ribosome, or break DNA.

## The cell wall drugs

**Penicillins** block cell wall building. Amoxicillin covers strep throat, ear infections, and Lyme disease; ampicillin adds Listeria coverage, which is why it appears in meningitis orders for the very young and very old. Piperacillin-tazobactam is the broad IV version that covers Pseudomonas and anaerobes. Signature harm: allergy, from rash to anaphylaxis.

**Cephalosporins** are penicillin's cousins, sorted by generation. First generation (cefazolin, cephalexin) is skin and soft tissue. Third generation (ceftriaxone) crosses into the brain and is the emergency department workhorse for pneumonia, pyelonephritis, and meningitis at `2 g` IV. Fourth generation (cefepime) picks up Pseudomonas. Signature harm: allergy, plus confusion at high doses in kidney failure with cefepime.

**Carbapenems** (meropenem, ertapenem) are the big guns held in reserve for resistant gram-negatives. Overuse breeds resistance, so they are not started casually.

**Vancomycin** kills gram-positives including MRSA and is given IV for bloodstream and skin infections, or orally for C. difficile only, since oral vancomycin stays in the gut. Signature harms: kidney injury, so trough levels are followed, and an infusion-rate histamine reaction with flushing of the face and chest that is not an allergy and resolves by slowing the infusion.

## The ribosome and DNA drugs

| Class | Example | Covers | Signature harm |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fluoroquinolones | ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin | gram-negatives, urinary, atypicals | tendon rupture, QT prolongation, aortic aneurysm, C. difficile |
| Macrolides | azithromycin | atypicals, respiratory | QT prolongation, GI upset |
| Aminoglycosides | gentamicin, tobramycin | serious gram-negatives | kidney injury and permanent hearing loss |
| Tetracyclines | doxycycline | tick-borne illness, atypicals, MRSA skin | photosensitivity, avoid in pregnancy and under `8` years |
| Nitroimidazoles | metronidazole | anaerobes, C. difficile, trichomonas | severe reaction with alcohol, metallic taste |
| Sulfonamides | trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole | urinary, MRSA skin | raises potassium and creatinine, sulfa allergy, Stevens-Johnson |
| Lincosamides | clindamycin | anaerobes above the diaphragm, MRSA | the highest C. difficile risk |

## The allergy conversation

Most people who say penicillin allergy do not have one. Nausea, diarrhea, or a headache is an intolerance, not an allergy. A family history is not an allergy. A childhood rash decades ago is almost never a true IgE allergy, and even confirmed penicillin allergy carries only about a `1%` to `2%` cross-reaction risk with modern cephalosporins.

> **Key:** The question that matters is what happened and when: hives, swelling, wheeze, or a drop in blood pressure means a real allergy, and the patient needs a different class. Vomiting after amoxicillin in third grade does not.

> **On shift:** Document the reaction, not just the word allergy. Writing down hives within 20 minutes versus upset stomach changes what the patient can safely receive for the rest of their life.

## C. difficile

Any antibiotic can wipe out the normal colon flora and let Clostridioides difficile overgrow, producing watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, and a high white count. Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and broad cephalosporins are the worst offenders. Treatment is oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, and hands must be washed with soap and water because alcohol gel does not kill the spores.
keyPoints: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV is the emergency department workhorse; ampicillin is added when Listeria is a concern.
Vancomycin covers MRSA, needs trough levels, and its flushing reaction is infusion-rate related, not an allergy.
Fluoroquinolones rupture tendons and prolong QT; aminoglycosides damage kidneys and hearing; metronidazole reacts with alcohol.
Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and cephalosporins carry the highest C. difficile risk; alcohol gel does not kill the spores.
True penicillin allergy is uncommon and cross-reacts with modern cephalosporins only about 1-2% of the time.

checks.q: A patient receiving vancomycin develops flushing and itching of the face, neck, and upper chest 20 minutes into the infusion, with normal blood pressure and no wheeze. The correct action is:
choices: Stop vancomycin permanently and label the chart as an allergy
Give epinephrine 0.3 mg IM immediately
Slow the infusion and pretreat with an antihistamine; this is a rate-related histamine reaction, not an allergy
Switch to a carbapenem
checks.why: Vancomycin infusion reaction is direct histamine release driven by infusion speed, and it resolves when the rate is slowed. Labeling it an allergy wrongly removes a needed drug. Epinephrine is for true anaphylaxis with airway or circulatory compromise, which is absent here.

checks.q: Which antibiotic carries the highest risk of causing Clostridioides difficile colitis?
choices: Clindamycin
Doxycycline
Nitrofurantoin
Azithromycin
checks.why: Clindamycin is the classic and highest-risk C. difficile offender, with fluoroquinolones and broad cephalosporins close behind. Doxycycline, nitrofurantoin, and azithromycin disturb colonic flora far less.

checks.q: A patient says he is allergic to penicillin. Which reported reaction most strongly suggests a true IgE-mediated allergy?
choices: Nausea and diarrhea for two days after starting amoxicillin
Hives and lip swelling within 30 minutes of the first dose
His mother is allergic to penicillin
A headache after each dose
checks.why: Hives, swelling, wheeze, or hypotension beginning within an hour is the pattern of true IgE-mediated allergy. Nausea, diarrhea, and headache are intolerances, and a family history is not an allergy at all.

lessons.title: Blood thinners, clot busters, and their antidotes
lessons.body:
## Two kinds of clot, two kinds of drug

In a fast-flowing artery a clot is mostly platelets stuck together, a white clot. In a slow vein it is mostly fibrin and trapped red cells, a red clot. That is why arterial disease (heart attack, most strokes) is treated with **antiplatelets**, and venous disease (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, clots thrown from a fibrillating atrium) is treated with **anticoagulants**.

## Anticoagulants

**Unfractionated heparin** supercharges antithrombin, which then shuts down thrombin and factor Xa. It is given IV, works instantly, and is out of the body in `1-2` hours, which makes it the choice when a procedure may be needed. Typical order: `80 units/kg` bolus, then `18 units/kg/h`, adjusted by aPTT or anti-Xa level. Two harms matter: bleeding, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, in which platelets fall by more than half around day `5-10` and the patient paradoxically clots. Reversal is protamine sulfate.

**Enoxaparin** is a low molecular weight heparin that inhibits mostly factor Xa. Its effect is predictable, so no routine monitoring: `1 mg/kg` SubQ every `12` hours to treat, `40 mg` daily to prevent. It is cleared by the kidney, so the dose is cut when creatinine clearance falls below `30 mL/min`, and protamine reverses it only partially.

**Warfarin** blocks the recycling of vitamin K, so the liver cannot finish factors II, VII, IX, and X. It takes `3-5` days to work and is measured by INR, target `2-3` for atrial fibrillation and venous clots, `2.5-3.5` for a mechanical mitral valve. Reversal for serious bleeding is vitamin K `10 mg` IV plus four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate.

**Direct oral anticoagulants** need no monitoring and have far fewer food and drug interactions. Apixaban and rivaroxaban block factor Xa; dabigatran blocks thrombin directly. Reversal is andexanet alfa for the Xa inhibitors and idarucizumab for dabigatran.

## Antiplatelets

Aspirin permanently disables cyclooxygenase inside the platelet, so no thromboxane A2 is made for that platelet's entire `7-10` day life. In suspected heart attack the dose is `324 mg` chewed, because chewing speeds absorption.

Clopidogrel blocks the platelet P2Y12 receptor. It is a prodrug needing CYP2C19, so some people never activate it. Ticagrelor is reversible, works faster, and causes a strange transient shortness of breath. Prasugrel is the most potent and the most bleeding-prone.

## Thrombolytics

Alteplase and tenecteplase convert plasminogen to plasmin, which dissolves fibrin that has already formed. They do not prevent clot; they destroy it. Uses are ischemic stroke within `4.5` hours (alteplase `0.9 mg/kg`, maximum `90 mg`), massive pulmonary embolism, and ST-elevation heart attack where catheterization is not available within `120` minutes.

> **Key:** The contraindication list all points one direction: anywhere a clot is currently holding back bleeding, dissolving it is fatal. Prior intracranial hemorrhage ever, ischemic stroke in the last `3` months, known aneurysm or vascular malformation, active internal bleeding, suspected aortic dissection, significant head trauma or major surgery within `3` months, blood pressure above `185/110`, and platelets below `100,000`.

## The reversal table

| Drug | Reversal |
|---|---|
| Unfractionated heparin | protamine sulfate |
| Enoxaparin | protamine (partial only) |
| Warfarin | vitamin K `10 mg` IV plus 4-factor PCC |
| Apixaban, rivaroxaban | andexanet alfa (or PCC if unavailable) |
| Dabigatran | idarucizumab |
| Aspirin, clopidogrel | platelet transfusion, desmopressin in uremia |
| Alteplase | cryoprecipitate, tranexamic acid, stop the drug |

> **On shift:** Ask every bleeding or head-injured patient which blood thinner they take and when the last dose was. A head CT in an anticoagulated patient with even minor head trauma is a different level of urgency, and the reversal agent is chosen from that one answer.
keyPoints: Antiplatelets treat arterial platelet-rich clots; anticoagulants treat venous fibrin-rich clots.
Heparin 80 units/kg bolus then 18 units/kg/h, reversed by protamine; watch for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia at day 5-10.
Warfarin targets INR 2-3, takes 3-5 days, and is reversed with vitamin K plus 4-factor PCC.
Aspirin 324 mg chewed in suspected heart attack disables platelets for their full 7-10 day life.
Thrombolytic contraindications all share one logic: never dissolve a clot that is holding back bleeding.

checks.q: A patient on heparin for 6 days has a platelet count that fell from 240,000 to 90,000 and a new leg clot. The most likely problem is:
choices: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which requires stopping all heparin
Heparin overdose causing bleeding into the leg
Dilution from IV fluids
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura unrelated to heparin
checks.why: A platelet drop of more than 50% at day 5-10 of heparin plus new thrombosis is the classic picture of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, an antibody reaction that paradoxically causes clotting. All heparin, including flushes, must stop and a non-heparin anticoagulant substituted. Overdose would cause bleeding, not clotting.

checks.q: Which finding absolutely rules out thrombolytics for an acute ischemic stroke?
choices: Blood pressure 168/96 after treatment
Age 79
Ischemic stroke 6 weeks ago
A blood glucose of 180 mg/dL
checks.why: An ischemic stroke within the last 3 months is an absolute contraindication because the recently infarcted brain bleeds readily. Blood pressure only disqualifies above 185/110, advanced age alone is not a contraindication, and a glucose of 180 is not a barrier.

checks.q: A patient on apixaban arrives with a large intracranial hemorrhage. The specific reversal agent is:
choices: Protamine sulfate
Idarucizumab
Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma
Andexanet alfa
checks.why: Apixaban is a factor Xa inhibitor, reversed by andexanet alfa, with prothrombin complex concentrate as the fallback. Protamine reverses heparins, idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, and vitamin K only works on warfarin because it acts through vitamin K dependent factor synthesis.

lessons.title: Cardiovascular drugs, pressors, and IV fluids
lessons.body:
## Blood pressure is flow times resistance

Pressure comes from how much blood the heart pumps out (cardiac output) and how tight the vessels are (systemic vascular resistance). Every cardiovascular drug moves one of those two numbers, and the receptor it hits tells you which.

## Slowing and relaxing the heart

**Beta blockers** block beta-1 on the heart: slower rate, weaker squeeze, lower oxygen demand. Metoprolol `5 mg` IV every `5` minutes up to three doses controls rate; labetalol blocks alpha and beta together, which makes it a hypertensive emergency drug at `10-20 mg` IV; esmolol lasts only `9` minutes, so it is the drip to use when you may want to undo it. Cautions: bradycardia and heart block, non-selective agents worsen asthma, and they blunt the shakiness that warns a diabetic of low sugar. Overdose is treated with glucagon.

**Calcium channel blockers** stop calcium from entering cells. Diltiazem and verapamil act on the heart and the AV node, so diltiazem `0.25 mg/kg` IV is standard for atrial fibrillation with a fast rate. Amlodipine acts only on vessels and is a daily blood pressure pill. Avoid diltiazem and verapamil in a weak heart and in atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White.

**ACE inhibitors** (lisinopril) stop angiotensin I becoming angiotensin II, so vessels relax and the kidney stops retaining salt. Three signatures: a dry cough in about `10%` from bradykinin buildup, angioedema of the lips and tongue that can arrive after years on the drug, and a rising potassium. ARBs (losartan) do the same job at the receptor without the cough. Neither is ever used in pregnancy.

**Nitrates** dilate veins, so less blood returns to the heart and the workload falls. Nitroglycerin `0.4 mg` sublingual every `5` minutes up to three doses, then a drip.

> **Trap:** Nitroglycerin plus a PDE-5 inhibitor causes catastrophic hypotension. Ask about sildenafil or vardenafil in the last `24` hours and tadalafil in the last `48` hours. Be equally careful in an inferior heart attack with right ventricular involvement, where the patient needs preload.

**Diuretics**: furosemide `40 mg` IV pulls fluid off and drops potassium; hydrochlorothiazide drops sodium; spironolactone spares potassium and can raise it dangerously.

**Digoxin** slows the AV node and strengthens contraction. Its range is tiny (`0.5-2.0 ng/mL`), toxicity brings nausea, confusion, and yellow-green halos around lights, low potassium makes it worse, and the antidote is digoxin immune Fab.

**Statins** block cholesterol synthesis; the harm to know is muscle breakdown, multiplied by CYP3A4 inhibitors and grapefruit.

## Antiarrhythmics

- **Amiodarone**: `150 mg` over `10` minutes for stable ventricular tachycardia, `300 mg` IV push in cardiac arrest. Blocks nearly every channel; long-term it poisons thyroid, lung, and liver.
- **Adenosine**: `6 mg` rapid IV push into a proximal vein with an immediate `20 mL` flush, then `12 mg`. It stops the heart for about `6` seconds to reset an SVT. Warn the patient about a moment of chest pressure and a feeling of doom.
- **Lidocaine**: `1-1.5 mg/kg` IV, the alternative to amiodarone in ventricular arrhythmia.
- **Procainamide**: the preferred drug for stable wide-complex tachycardia and for atrial fibrillation with pre-excitation.

## Pressors and inotropes, chosen by receptor

| Drug | Receptors | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Norepinephrine | alpha-1 over beta-1 | first-line in septic shock and most undifferentiated shock |
| Epinephrine | alpha and beta equally | anaphylaxis `0.3 mg` IM, arrest `1 mg` IV every `3-5` min |
| Vasopressin | V1, no adrenergic receptor | fixed `0.03 units/min` added to norepinephrine |
| Phenylephrine | pure alpha-1 | when tachycardia is the problem; causes reflex bradycardia |
| Dopamine | dose-dependent | mostly replaced; more arrhythmia than norepinephrine |
| Dobutamine | beta-1 | pure inotrope for cardiogenic shock; can drop blood pressure |

Push-dose pressors are tiny syringe doses for a short gap, such as phenylephrine `100 mcg` or epinephrine `10-20 mcg` after intubation drops the pressure. For hypertensive emergencies the drips are nicardipine or clevidipine, with labetalol and hydralazine as pushes; the goal is lowering mean arterial pressure by about `25%` in the first hour, not normalizing it.

## Fluids are drugs too

| Fluid | What it is | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Normal saline `0.9%` | `154 mEq/L` each of sodium and chloride | resuscitation; large volumes cause a chloride-driven acidosis |
| Lactated Ringer's | balanced, closer to plasma | preferred for large-volume resuscitation |
| D5W | free water once the sugar burns off | a diluent, not a resuscitation fluid |
| `3%` saline | hypertonic | seizing patient with severe low sodium, `100 mL` bolus |
| Blood products | oxygen carrying and clotting | hemorrhage; fluids alone do not carry oxygen |
keyPoints: Norepinephrine is first-line in septic shock; epinephrine is 0.3 mg IM for anaphylaxis and 1 mg IV in arrest.
Adenosine 6 mg must be pushed fast with a 20 mL flush and causes about 6 seconds of asystole.
Nitroglycerin with sildenafil or vardenafil in 24 hours (tadalafil 48) causes catastrophic hypotension.
ACE inhibitors give cough, angioedema, and hyperkalemia; diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg controls atrial fibrillation rate.
Lactated Ringer's is preferred over large volumes of normal saline, which causes hyperchloremic acidosis.

checks.q: A 58-year-old with chest pain took tadalafil last night. The physician asks for nitroglycerin. The correct response is:
choices: Give it; the interaction only applies to sildenafil
Flag the tadalafil, because the interaction lasts about 48 hours and can cause profound hypotension
Give half the usual dose to be safe
Give it only if the blood pressure is above 160 systolic
checks.why: PDE-5 inhibitors and nitrates both raise cyclic GMP, and the combination can drop blood pressure catastrophically. Tadalafil's window is about 48 hours, longer than the 24 hours for sildenafil and vardenafil. Halving the dose or using a pressure threshold does not make the combination safe.

checks.q: Which vasopressor is first-line for septic shock that remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation?
choices: Dopamine
Dobutamine
Norepinephrine
Phenylephrine
checks.why: Norepinephrine is the guideline first-line agent: strong alpha-1 vasoconstriction with some beta-1 support, and fewer arrhythmias than dopamine. Dobutamine is an inotrope that lowers blood pressure, and phenylephrine is a narrow-use pure vasoconstrictor.

checks.q: Adenosine 6 mg is ordered for stable SVT. The most important administration detail is:
choices: Push it rapidly into a proximal IV followed immediately by a 20 mL flush
Infuse it over 10 minutes to avoid asystole
Dilute it in 100 mL and run it over an hour
Give it IM if IV access is difficult
checks.why: Adenosine has a half-life of under 10 seconds, so a slow push is metabolized before it reaches the AV node and does nothing. It must be pushed fast into a proximal vein with an immediate flush, and the expected brief asystole is the mechanism, not a complication.

lessons.title: Lungs, sugar, gut, and the drugs you will see every shift
lessons.body:
## Respiratory

**Albuterol**, a beta-2 agonist, relaxes bronchial muscle within minutes: `2.5 mg` nebulized, or continuous in severe asthma. Expect tremor, a fast heart rate, and a small potassium drop, which is why it also treats hyperkalemia. **Ipratropium** `0.5 mg` blocks muscarinic receptors and adds benefit in the first hours.

**Steroids** do not open the airway; they switch off the inflammation underneath and take `4-6` hours, which is exactly why they go in early: prednisone `40-60 mg` PO, methylprednisolone `125 mg` IV, or dexamethasone `10 mg`.

**Magnesium sulfate** `2 g` IV over `20` minutes is the next escalation. **Epinephrine** `0.3 mg` IM treats anaphylaxis or an asthmatic too tight to move air. Croup gets **dexamethasone** `0.6 mg/kg` plus racemic epinephrine, then watching for rebound stridor.

## Endocrine

| Insulin | Onset | Peak | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lispro, aspart (rapid) | `15` min | `1` h | `3-5` h |
| Regular | `30-60` min | `2-4` h | `6-8` h |
| NPH (intermediate) | `1-2` h | `4-8` h | `12-18` h |
| Glargine, detemir (long) | `1-2` h | no real peak | `20-24` h |

Only regular insulin goes in a drip, at `0.1 units/kg/h` in diabetic ketoacidosis, and never before potassium is known, because insulin drives potassium into cells.

Low sugar is reversed with `25 g` of dextrose (one `50 mL` D50 syringe) or `250 mL` of D10, which is gentler on veins. Without IV access, glucagon `1 mg` IM works in `10-15` minutes by releasing liver glycogen, so it fails in a starved or alcoholic patient. An awake patient gets `15 g` of oral glucose.

Metformin causes lactic acidosis when it accumulates, so it is held around contrast and in kidney injury. Sulfonylureas cause hours of hypoglycemia, so those patients are admitted rather than fed and released. Hydrocortisone `100 mg` IV treats adrenal crisis.

## Gastrointestinal

Pantoprazole `40 mg` IV shuts the acid pump; famotidine `20 mg` blocks H2 more gently. Ondansetron `4 mg` blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the vomiting center and prolongs the QT. Metoclopramide `10 mg` also blocks dopamine, so it causes dystonia and restlessness. Promethazine leaking from a vein causes tissue necrosis and limb loss, so it is diluted into a large running line or avoided. Octreotide `50 mcg` IV then `50 mcg/h` constricts splanchnic vessels in variceal bleeding.

> **On shift:** The GI cocktail of antacid with viscous lidocaine relieves some upper abdominal pain, but relief never proves the pain is not cardiac.
